d_open: They carried me out of that house at one in the morning. I am a doctor. ... I went there to expose a fraud.
d_s1: I was a young surgeon then, in Sunderland. The stories coming out of Willington Mill, I thought nonsense, frankly. So I wrote to Mr Procter, and asked leave to sit up one night, and detect the imposture. [exhales] I took a friend — and a brace of pistols, in my coat. I meant to let one fall in front of the miller. As if by accident.
d_s2: We took the landing, on the third storey. Midnight came, and nothing. [pause] Then, ten minutes to twelve — a pattering. Like a number of people, walking on bare feet, across the floor. Then knocking — knuckles, rapping among our very feet. [exhales] And then a cough. A hollow cough... out of the empty room.
d_s3: Ten minutes to one. I looked at my watch, and as I lifted my eyes — the closet door opened. [pause] A female figure came out of it. Grey garments. Head bent down. One hand pressed to her chest, as if she were in pain. The other hand pointing... downwards. [exhales] She came across that floor. Slow. Cautious steps. ... And her hand went out. Towards my sleeping friend.
d_s4: I rushed at her. Mr Procter says I gave the most awful yell he ever heard — I remember none of it. I went straight through where she stood, and I fell upon my friend. And after that, for very nearly three hours... I can give no account of myself. [pause] They carried me down the stairs. A grown man. A surgeon. In — his words — an agony of fear and terror.
d_s5: I wrote it all down for Mr Procter, ten days after. When my hand was steady enough. And at the bottom of the letter I certified it — this account is strictly true, and correct, in every respect. [pause] I went in with two loaded pistols, to catch a man. There was no man. ... You cannot shoot what came out of that closet. [exhales] And I never went back.
